subtitulo: Disagreeing with a sales pitch you half believe
descripcion: English separates the strength of a disagreement from its social temperature more sharply than Spanish does. You can reject an idea completely and still sound collaborative, and the mechanism is almost entirely formulaic — which means it is learnable in a week. The core move: attack the idea, never the person, and always leave the other position somewhere to stand.

filas: Help me understand how that would work in practice.
you suspect it collapses and want them to find it
I see it differently, and here's why.
I'd challenge the assumption underneath that.
the logic is fine, the starting point isn't
I hear you, but I don't think that follows.
I'm going to push back on that.
direct but still not hostile; very standard
reserve for when you mean it

ejemplos.texto: *I'd challenge the assumption underneath that rather than the conclusion — you're assuming the failure mode is technical.*
*Help me understand how that would work with a 200-millisecond budget.*
*I hear you, but I don't think the second half follows from the first.*
*I'm going to push back on that.*
*That's true of small systems, less so of anything safety-critical.*

notas: *I'm afraid I disagree* is textbook English and sounds slightly antique in speech. Fine in writing.
Attacking the *assumption* rather than the *conclusion* is the highest-value C1 move: it lets the other person retreat without losing face.
*With respect* is a warning sign in British English — it almost always precedes a demolition. Use knowingly or not at all.

es.en: Spanish softens disagreement with formulas like «no sé si estoy del todo de acuerdo», which corresponds well to I'm not sure I entirely agree. A literal «no estoy de acuerdo» (I don't agree) sounds blunter in English professional contexts than it usually does in Spanish.
es.es: El español suaviza el desacuerdo con fórmulas como «no sé si estoy del todo de acuerdo», que corresponde bien a «I'm not sure I entirely agree». El literal «no estoy de acuerdo» («I don't agree») suena más brusco en contextos profesionales ingleses de lo que suele sonar en español.

de.en: «Das sehe ich etwas anders» corresponds exactly to I see it slightly differently, a very useful diplomatic formula. The literal I am of another opinion sounds stiff; I'm not sure I agree is the natural English choice.
de.de: «Das sehe ich etwas anders» entspricht genau «I see it slightly differently» und ist eine sehr nützliche diplomatische Formel. Das wörtliche «I am of another opinion» klingt steif; natürlicher ist «I'm not sure I agree».

it.en: «Non sono del tutto d'accordo» corresponds well to I don't entirely agree, and «la vedo un po' diversamente» to I see it slightly differently. Diplomatic disagreement therefore transfers directly.
it.it: «Non sono del tutto d'accordo» corrisponde bene a «I don't entirely agree», e «la vedo un po' diversamente» a «I see it slightly differently». Il disaccordo diplomatico si trasferisce quindi direttamente.

fr.en: «Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord» corresponds well to I don't entirely agree, and «je vois les choses un peu différemment» to I see it slightly differently. Diplomatic disagreement therefore transfers directly.
fr.fr: «Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord» correspond bien à «I don't entirely agree», et «je vois les choses un peu différemment» à «I see it slightly differently». Le désaccord diplomatique se transfère donc directement.

pt.en: «Não concordo inteiramente» corresponds well to I don't entirely agree, and «vejo isso de outra forma» to I see it differently. Diplomatic disagreement therefore transfers directly.
pt.pt: «Não concordo inteiramente» corresponde bem a «I don't entirely agree», e «vejo isso de outra forma» a «I see it differently». O desacordo diplomático, portanto, se transfere diretamente.

errores: *You are wrong* — grammatically fine, socially expensive, rare in professional English.
Softening until the disagreement disappears. If nobody noticed you disagreed, you didn't.
*No, but…* as an opener. Reverse it: *Yes, and here's the difficulty…*

es: *I am not agree* — a fossilised Spanish-speaker error worth naming once and killing.
de: Carrying over German directness: *That's not correct* or *I disagree* with no cushioning, which is neutral in German meetings but sounds combative in English.
it: «*Guarda, …*» as an opener rendered as *Look, …*, which sounds confrontational in English, instead of *I see it a bit differently*.
fr: «*Écoute, …*» as an opener rendered as *Listen, …*, which sounds confrontational in English, instead of *I see it a bit differently*.
pt: «*Olha, …*» as an opener rendered as *Look, …*, which sounds confrontational in English, instead of *I see it a bit differently*.

mision.consigna: A friend is about to splash out on something expensive because it's on special offer. Talk them out of it without making them feel stupid.
requisitos: four different disagreement formulas from the reference box
one *Yes, and the difficulty is…* that accepts their point first
never start a sentence with *No* or *But*

microtareas.texto: Write down the last *purchase decision* you regret. What argument would have stopped you?
Rewrite three blunt objections (*That's a waste of money*) as *Help me understand how…* questions.
Record 90 seconds disagreeing with: *Buying cheap is always the smart choice.* Use *to shop on impulse*.

autochequeo: Did I attack an assumption, or only the conclusion?
Would a reader know I disagreed, or did I soften it away?
Any sentence that would read as rude to a British or American colleague?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on how I disagree. (1) Mark each disagreement formula and rate its social temperature from 1 to 5. (2) Tell me whether I attacked the assumption or only the conclusion. (3) Flag anywhere I softened so much the disagreement vanished. (4) Flag anything that would read as rude. Do not rewrite the text.
